name: Transactional Outbox
intent: Make 'save to the database' and 'publish an event' succeed or fail together, by writing the event to the database in the same transaction and publishing it afterwards.
scenario: When an order is placed, the service must save it to its database and publish an OrderPlaced event so other services react. The database and the message broker are two separate systems.
problem: Saving to the database and publishing to the broker are two writes to two systems, and no transaction covers both (the dual-write problem). If the app crashes between them, or the broker is down, you get an order with no event, so downstream services never learn of it. Publishing first is no better: an event can announce an order that was never saved.

howItWorks.title: Write the event into an outbox table
howItWorks.text: Inside the same database transaction that saves the order, insert a row into an 'outbox' table describing the event. Because it is one transaction, either both the order and its event are saved, or neither is.

howItWorks.title: A relay publishes from the outbox
howItWorks.text: A separate process (the relay) reads unsent outbox rows and publishes them to the broker, then marks them as sent. It can poll the table, or follow the database's change log (change data capture).

howItWorks.title: If the broker is down, events wait safely
howItWorks.text: The rows stay in the outbox, so nothing is lost. When the broker returns, the relay sends them. The order is already saved and the user is not blocked.

howItWorks.title: Delivery is at least once
howItWorks.text: If the relay crashes after publishing but before marking the row as sent, it will publish it again. Consumers must therefore be idempotent, for example by remembering the event ids they have already processed.

howItWorks.title: Housekeeping
howItWorks.text: Sent rows are deleted or archived periodically. Events keep a stable order per entity, and each carries a unique id so consumers can detect duplicates.

pros: No lost events and no phantom events: the database and the event stay consistent
The service stays available when the broker is temporarily down
Works with ordinary databases, with no distributed transaction needed
Simple to reason about and to monitor (count the unsent rows)
cons: Events are published slightly later, not instantly
Duplicates are possible, so every consumer must be idempotent
An extra table and relay process to build and operate
Polling adds database load unless change data capture is used
whenToUse: A service changes its own database and must reliably announce the change
Losing an event, or sending one for a change that did not happen, is unacceptable
You publish domain events to other services, search indexes or analytics
whenNotToUse: Events are non-critical and an occasional loss is acceptable
The data and the messaging already share one transactional system
Immediate publication matters more than reliability and consumers can tolerate gaps
pitfalls: Consumers that are not idempotent, so a duplicate sends two emails or charges twice
Letting the outbox table grow forever
Publishing from the application after commit 'just this once', bringing the dual write back
Several relay instances publishing the same row without coordination
